notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0180a.stoa007.opp-l: Scanning errors corrected silently where evident (e.g. nefas for 'netas', Petavius for 'Pelavius', ederet for 'odoret', improprie for 'impropris', factum for 'jactum'). The garbled Greek 'νχΐτιτά' is taken as πρός τι, 'relative', glossed by the following 'et relative'. 'catholicae quidem dici' is read as 'catholice quidem dici', 'said in a Catholic sense'. In line 2, 'Haec verba vero non ad se dubiae subsunt interpretationi' is read as 'the words "not towards himself" are open to doubtful interpretation'.

Several evident scanning errors were read as intended: 'praefalis' as 'praefatis', 'nolant' as 'notant', 'Disserit.' as 'Dissert.', 'eujus' as 'cujus', 'ad in' as 'ad an.', 'ivepysiat' as Greek ἐνέργειαι, 'ύιοπάτορα' as υἱοπάτορα, 'intensus' as 'infensus' (hostile). In the Vienna title, 'Presbyter scribit sibi' is evidently garbled; the Ballerini's suggested reading is given as the text indicates. 'de se sius initio genitum' is corrupt; rendered as 'de Filio sine initio genitum' ([of the Son,] begotten without beginning), in line with the glossary and the earlier discussion. 'rem veri crescere' rendered as 'the cause of truth was growing'; it may stand for 'rem vere crescere'. 'Schisma Ursicini' is the schism of Ursinus (Ursicinus), rival of Damasus.

In the Lucifer text, 'non ad se factum' corresponds to 'genitum, non factum' in Faustinus' version; the editor treats such variants as corruptions, and the phrase is rendered literally. In 2.1 'commutant' is translated as printed; 'commendant' (commend) may be intended. In 2.3 'contra impiam fidem sentiunt' is awkward ('they hold an impious [view] against the faith'?); rendered by sense. Footnote letters (a–j) omitted.

nodes.text: APPENDIX. ON THE PROFESSION OF FAITH OF ST LUCIFER, BISHOP OF CAGLIARI.

We first learned of this very ancient fragment, which we append here, from the *Diarium Italicum* of the celebrated Bernard de Montfaucon, who testifies that he saw it at Milan in the Ambrosian Library, in these words, p. 19: "A codex of the eighth century in Lombardic script contains certain homilies of Chrysostom; certain [works] of Eucherius of Lyons; the Confession of Faith of Lucifer; likewise the Confession of Athanasius, which is found among the spurious [works] attributed to Vigilius; likewise the Faith of Ambrose." So when we had asked by letter for a copy of it from the distinguished Baldassare Oltrocchi, Prefect of the Ambrosian Library, he very kindly sent it to us, and of his own accord passed on what we needed both for determining the age of the codex in which the Faith of Lucifer is copied and for judging whether it is a genuine work of the holy bishop. The codex, then, is of parchment, and is written in a round, minuscule Roman hand, with the letters joined to one another within each word. It contains certain shorter works of St John Chrysostom, to whom, however, the title "Saint" is not prefixed in the codex; part of the book of Hermas entitled the Shepherd; various small works of St Eucherius; and then several Professions of Faith. These are: the Faith of St Ambrose, Bishop; likewise the Catholic Faith; the Faith of St Lucifer, Bishop; the Faith which proceeded from the Council of Nicaea; the Faith of Blessed Athanasius, which differs entirely from the Creed published under his name, and which Montfaucon states has been printed among the spurious [works] attributed to Vigilius. Finally, the titles themselves and the first line of each small work are painted in red. From these [features] Oltrocchi infers that the whole codex is much older than the one from which Ludovico Antonio Muratori drew the Faith of Bachiarius and the Exposition of the Catholic Faith, or Creed, of Venantius Fortunatus, and published them among the *Anecdota* which he had collected from the Ambrosian Library. And whereas that codex is said by Muratori to have been written a thousand years ago, Oltrocchi declares himself more cautious than he, since he judges that the codex from which he copied the Faith of Lucifer should be assigned to the sixth century at least, although it could appear, and be called, older. Oltrocchi therefore disagrees with Montfaucon both in fixing the age of the codex and in identifying the form of the script; nor can we come over to the opinion of either, since, being absent, we cannot see the codex itself and examine it carefully. Yet if we consider only the antiquity of the codex, the judgement of those who held that this record of Lucifer's Faith had once been written or dictated by Lucifer himself would perhaps not be objectionable. But there are not a few things, nor slight ones, in the Formula of Faith itself which prevent us from embracing an opinion of this kind.

For first, the style itself and the manner of writing differ greatly from Lucifer's. Then, Lucifer uses no Formula of Faith other than the Nicene, which he set out in full in the book *On Not Sparing Those Who Offend against God*, and whose opening he repeats in the book entitled *That One Must Die for the Son of God*. Next, the expressions he generally uses when discussing the divine nature of the Word certainly differ from those which this Formula of Faith presents; in it, moreover, the word *homoousios* is omitted, although its force and sense can be detected in it, whereas Lucifer himself openly presses this word and its meaning in his books, and throws it at Constantius. For the word *homoousios* was for Catholics a sure token of faith, which it would have been impious at that time to omit in Formulas of Faith and in books written against the Arians. And indeed, at whatever time or place Lucifer might have published this Formula of Faith, it would be astonishing that a most learned bishop, who knew well all the arts, tricks and snares of the Arians, and who fought so long and so bravely to defend that God the Son is *homoousios* with God the Father, that is, Consubstantial, should in the end, in a public testimony of his Faith, have refrained from the one word which confirmed Catholic doctrine; and much more astonishing if he had used the truly ambiguous expressions which this Formula contains, since they had to be guarded against above all at that time in a matter of such moment, and we find that Lucifer scarcely used them. Of this kind, then, is the expression by which the Father is said to have the Son "made from himself without beginning, not towards himself". For the Synod of Nicaea decreed that the word "make" must be excluded from the divine generation of the Son, whom it clearly taught to be begotten, not made; and the writer of this Faith himself is in some way inconsistent, since he adds a little further on that the Son is begotten, not made. Now although, with the added words "from himself" and "without beginning", a Catholic sense can be drawn from the expression, the use of this word is certainly imprudent: it is indeed sometimes read in the sacred books where the Son of God is spoken of, but the Fathers teach, against the calumnies of the Arians, that it is to be attributed to his human nature, as Petavius argues in book II *On the Trinity*, chapter 3. Nor is the other expression, "from himself", free of ambiguity, since it can signify both an efficient principle and a begetting and producing one. The latter rightly befits God the Father, who is truly the principle begetting the Son; not so the former, since being made is incompatible with the Son of God. On this Petavius argues against the Calvinists in book VI, chapter 11, where he warns: "Behold, this futile hunting after words and syllables, which nevertheless tends to no simple or moderate evil" (says Basil, treating of these very little words in the book *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 2), "but has a deep and hidden design against piety." Hence, even if the participle "made" were referred only to these latter words, "not towards himself", these expressions would still be suspect and not to be approved, especially in a public testimony of the Catholic Faith; as the Synodical Letter of the Council of Alexandria also warned, to which Lucifer himself subscribed. Moreover, the Son, whose divine generation has the Father as its principle, is improperly said to be "without beginning"; but in a certain manner of writing or speaking less usual among the ancients, to be without beginning means the same as to be eternal, and so the Son is called *anarchos* [without beginning] because he is eternal and his generation is eternal; on which Petavius argues at length in book V, chapter 5. Lucifer too did indeed use this phrase "without beginning" in the book *That One Must Die for the Son of God*; but he sets it directly against the error of the Arians, who attributed a beginning to the Son because they said he was made and created by the Father. But the words "not towards himself" are open to doubtful interpretation. For the Father begets the Son towards himself, and in the Son those things may be considered which are relative, such as being the Word, and the image of the Father, and the very notion of Son; but the Son is not towards the Father if the discussion concerns what is predicated of the Son of God absolutely and according to substance; for the Son is God absolutely, and good, and wise, etc.; and the Petavius already cited investigates and explains much in this sense, following Augustine, in book IV, chapter 10, and book VII, chapter 9, no. 8. But the author of this Faith perhaps used these words to oppose the error of the Arians, who said that the Son, the Word, was a kind of instrument of the Father, which he had used to create everything else; and this impious opinion was followed above all by both Eusebiuses, of Nicomedia and of Caesarea, as Petavius attests in book II, chapter 3, no. 16, and chapter 7, no. 7. Hence they taught that the Father made the Son for himself, subject to himself and an instrumental servant; and therefore this Formula of Faith professes, with an obscure meaning of the words indeed, that the Father has the Son "not made towards himself". Yet you will scarcely find the use of this expression "towards himself" introduced in the time when Lucifer lived; it seems first to have begun to be adopted in the age of Augustine, and afterwards to have been drawn by theologians into various senses and various meanings. Noting these things, then, who would easily persuade himself that Lucifer could have publicly testified to his Faith in such ambiguous and obscure terms? Add to this that more is said about the Holy Spirit in this Formula, in a Catholic sense indeed, than in the others which were published in Lucifer's time, whether by Catholics or by heretics; and although the Arians themselves held impious views on the divinity of the Holy Spirit, yet before the Macedonian heresy neither councils nor Fathers defined anything about it in fuller words and statements, "since at that time the question had not been raised on that matter by name", says Petavius in book II, chapter 6, no. 4. But after the error of Macedonius was condemned by the Council of Constantinople in the year 381, people began to discuss the nature of the Holy Spirit more clearly and fully, and to use everywhere the phrases which this Formula displays; except, however, for the Council of Alexandria held in the year 362, whose Synodical Letter, written to the Antiochenes, expressly decreed that the Holy Spirit must be held to be God, and that he is not a creature, nor foreign to the substance of the Father and the Son, as Petavius indicates in book I, chapter 14, no. 18. Now Lucifer himself assented to this Council and its decrees, as was shown in his Life, § 7; and since the Alexandrian Fathers wished this also to be confirmed from the Synod of Sardica, that no one should write or publish anywhere any profession of Faith other than the Nicene, we certainly cannot persuade ourselves that so very useful and holy a decree, which he himself had approved, was neglected and violated by Lucifer himself. Nor indeed do we deny that Lucifer sometimes spoke of the Holy Spirit in his books, and fiercely attacked the impiety of the Arians on this point too, but with expressions and words unlike those put forward in this Formula, as is readily clear from our preface. Finally, we add this argument also, by which it may be proved that this Formula is not to be attributed to Lucifer as author: namely, that no time can rightly be fixed at which he would have had to confirm his Faith by a public and written testimony. For at the Council of Milan, which he attended as legate of Pope Liberius, he professed only the Nicene Formula of Faith before the Emperor Constantius, as he himself testifies in the book *That One Must Die for the Son of God* in these words: "We legates asserted in your palace, and have not ceased to affirm, that it has always been believed, and is believed, by Christians just as the sacred faith appears to have been written down at Nicaea against your Arian heresy and all errors"; and throughout the whole time of his exile he testified to the same Faith in books openly written, in the very words of the Nicene formula. After his return from exile, when he had devoted himself wholly to settling the dissensions of the Church of Antioch and of the province of Caesarea, which had arisen over the election of their bishops, he returned to his own Church in Sardinia; and what reason befell him there to compose and publish a new Formula of Faith, why one different from the Nicene, why ambiguous and obscure in some part of it, no one can guess, nor safely state. These are the arguments by which we rightly judge that someone other than Lucifer was the author of this Formula.

But all ambiguity about the author himself was removed for us when we saw almost the very same Formula of Faith already published earlier by Pasquier Quesnel in volume 2 of the Works of St Leo, Pope, in the Code of Ecclesiastical Canons, etc., chapter 38, and issued again from the Venetian press in volume 3 of the same Works, page 278, which were illustrated by the Ballerini brothers, with learned and erudite labour indeed, against Quesnel's errors. In its title this [Formula] bears the name of Faustinus the Presbyter, and it is the same one that Mabillon entitles *Breve Fidei* (Brief [Statement] of Faith) from the Reichenau manuscript, as the Ballerini testify; and this, as we suppose, is the same Reichenau codex which Mabillon in his *Iter Germanicum* reports having seen at Reichenau: "A remarkable book in large folio, in which are contained all the expositions of the Fathers on the Lord's Prayer, and also various Confessions of Faith." The Oxford manuscript, from which Quesnel published the Code of Canons, etc., shows this title: "The Faith of Faustinus the Presbyter sent to the Emperor Theodosius"; another, the Thuanus manuscript: "Likewise the confession of the true faith of Faustinus the Presbyter, which the Emperor Theodosius ordered to be written and sent by the aforesaid." Quesnel, in dissertation 14, no. 6, corrects [this to] "which by the aforesaid," etc., conjecturing that this Faith was written out by Faustinus at the order of Theodosius, and sent by Theodosius to Damasus, to be placed afterwards in the archives of the Apostolic See, whence it was transferred into the Roman Code. But the Ballerini reject Quesnel's opinion in the Preface to the new edition of this Code, which they judge to have been compiled neither in Italy nor at Rome, but in Gaul; and from the Vienna manuscript of the same Code they cite this title: "Likewise the confession of the true faith of Faustinus the Presbyter, which the Presbyter writes, [which] the Emperor Theodosius ordered to be sent to him"; the Ballerini note [that it should read] "wrote, and [ordered to be sent] to him," etc.

Three very ancient codices, therefore, attribute this Faith to Faustinus; and no other Faustinus is found, as Quesnel observes in the dissertation cited, who could have been the author of this booklet, besides that Luciferian presbyter Faustinus who, since he wrote seven books against the Arians and Macedonians addressed to Flaccilla, wife of the Emperor Theodosius, and together with the presbyter Marcellinus presented a petition (*Libellus precum*) to Theodosius himself, could easily have sent to the same Emperor a booklet bearing witness to his Faith: and with this opinion we indeed agree. As for the reason why Faustinus published a booklet of his Faith, Quesnel indicates it in the same place: namely, because he was harassed, together with his colleague, as a follower of the errors of Sabellius and Apollinaris, by Turbo, Bishop of Eleutheropolis, the city in which Faustinus was then living, having been driven from Rome with Marcellinus, himself also a Luciferian, on account of the schism of Ursinus. For Faustinus himself complains bitterly of Turbo, in his own name and Marcellinus', in the petition sent from Eleutheropolis to the Emperors, namely Valentinian, Theodosius and Arcadius, as in the Preface to the petition: "The excellent Turbo," he says, "Bishop of the city of Eleutheropolis, despising our lowliness... after he heard that certain people were joining themselves to the unimpaired Faith, and that by the grace of God the cause of truth was growing, threatens us with ruin and stirs up trouble." Whether Faustinus offered his Faith to Theodosius of his own accord, or at Theodosius' order, Quesnel fixes the time at which he published it not before the year 379, to which the beginning of Theodosius' reign is assigned, nor long after: because there is deep silence in it about Macedonius and about the First Council of Constantinople, by which he was condemned in the year 381, and also because it does not speak of the error against the Holy Spirit in any other way than that in which the Fathers of the Council of Alexandria wrote against that heretic in their Synodal Letter of the year 362. Le Quien, in volume 3 of the *Oriens Christianus*, among the Bishops of Eleutheropolis, seems in a certain way to refer the beginning of Turbo's episcopate to the same time, since he says that he held the episcopate until about the death of Theodosius, that is, to the year 395; but the year in which Eutychius, bishop before Turbo, died is unknown. Having found, then, the author of this Formula and the time at which it was written, and having learned the reason for writing it, let us see how little Quesnel's copy differs from ours. Faustinus there prefixes a short apology for why he himself wrote another [Faith] besides the Nicene, namely so that he should not seem to break the decrees of the Synod of Sardica, which the [Synod] of Alexandria had approved, forbidding new Formulas of Faith to be published by anyone thereafter; but this opening is absent from our copy from the Ambrosian codex. Then he testifies to his Faith in entirely the same words, except for these: "[of the Son,] begotten without beginning, not made"; whereas in the Ambrosian copy there is some obscurity and ambiguity in these [words], as we pointed out above. Finally, in a few words he defends himself against the charge of the Apollinarian heresy brought against him, and condemns those who confess three hypostases; and this closing clause is likewise lacking in the Ambrosian [copy]. Now Quesnel observes as follows: Faustinus, like his colleague Marcellinus, was infected with the Luciferian schism, and therefore opposed the decree of the Council of Alexandria, by which it had been ordained that those who had shared in Arian communion under the Emperor Constantius, especially bishops, should be received back into favour with the Catholics. Hence he was held suspect of the Sabellian and Apollinarian error. For the Fathers of the Synod of Alexandria had decreed that those who were returning to the Church from the fellowship of the Arians should also condemn the impious doctrines of Sabellius; next, that they should confess that the Holy Spirit is not a creature, nor alien, but proper to and undivided from the essence of the Father and the Son; and finally, that they should execrate the foolish error of Apollinaris, who had taught that the Word, the Son of God, had assumed to himself a body without a soul, and lacking sense and mind. Therefore Faustinus, so as not to seem to reject the Catholic doctrine set forth by the Alexandrian Fathers and approved by the consent of the whole Church, while he rejected the decree on receiving those who had returned from the Arians, condemns Sabellius by name, and against his error openly distinguishes the persons in the Trinity; he confesses that the nature of the Holy Spirit is divine in almost the very words of the Synod, and he clearly detests the heresy of Apollinaris; but about the indulgence granted to the lapsed he is entirely silent; and the use of [the term] three hypostases, of which the lapsed had been accused as though suspect of heresy before they obtained pardon, and whose correct and Catholic sense they had demonstrated to the Synod, he flatly denies is to be tolerated among Catholics. Hence another reason why he was called a Sabellian by those who confessed three hypostases in the Trinity, that is, three persons; for Sabellius asserted that God was *huiopatōr* (Son-Father), that is, that there is one person in God, Father and Son, as Athanasius says in his Exposition of the Faith; and he thought of the Holy Spirit just as of the Son, so as to make them *homotimous* (of equal honour), and not to separate them from the person of the Father, but to posit one and the same and, as it were, primary hypostasis, of which those two, the Son and the Holy Spirit, were *energeiai* (operations), as Petavius says in book I, chapter 6. But since the ancient Fathers, especially before the Council of Nicaea, used the Greek noun *hypostasis* for *ousia*, or essence, and since it does in fact signify both that which simply exists, that is, essence, and that which subsists by itself, namely an individual, or person (on which see Petavius, book IV, chapters 1, 4, 7), the Greek Fathers afterwards employed it in this sense of an individual, in which it was also employed by those who had returned from the Arians to the communion of the right Faith; for by the term three hypostases they understood not three essences, nor three Gods, nor three principles, but three persons in the Trinity: the Father, who truly is and subsists, the Son as existing and subsisting, and the Holy Spirit as subsisting and existing; which the Alexandrian Synodal Letter attests. Thus the disputes and quarrels which had then arisen over the word *hypostasis* had died down, especially at Antioch, whence the Antiochene schism was kindled, as Basil witnesses in letter 349 of the old edition, cited by Petavius, book IV, chapter 4, no. 11, when he writes to Count Terentius that he considers those questions, on account of which the schism was kindled at the beginning, to be of no small importance. In this place it should be noted that this dissension began first among the Eastern Greeks, not between Greeks and Latins, as the preface to the Synodal letters of the Council of Alexandria asserts, in volume 2 of the Councils, earlier Venetian edition. But at the time when Faustinus published this Faith, the fire of contention, once quenched, had already flared up more violently, and the Latins too were feeding it with great partisan zeal: for some wanted *ousia*, that is, essence or substance, to be understood by the word *hypostasis*; others person, or personal subsistence; and, interpreting substance among themselves, these as subsistence, those as essence, they contended over the very force of those same words in the Latin language. Wherefore Faustinus, since he maintained that essence is signified by the word substance, denies that three substances are to be declared in the Trinity; for it followed that those who confessed three substances in that sense would confess three Gods; and in writing out the Faith itself he seems to have repeated the word substance, insofar as it expresses essence, almost on purpose. But those who said that person is expressed by the word *hypostasis* accused Faustinus and his colleague Marcellinus of Sabellianism, since they seemed to them to defend one person in the Trinity. And from these things one may conjecture that Faustinus inserted mention of the three substances into the Formula of Faith for this reason too, namely to court the favour of Damasus, the Roman Pontiff, to whom he had been hostile in the schism of Ursinus; for Damasus had imposed silence on the controversy over the three *hypostaseis*, as Baronius holds under the year 372, from the letters of Cyril of Alexandria, and had come over to the opinion of Jerome, who disapproved of the use of [the term] three hypostases. However, since it is uncertain whether Faustinus was staying at Eleutheropolis when he published the Faith, as Quesnel thinks, or in another city, certainly in the East, where the contention over the use and sense of three hypostases was still raging, we are led by this to the conjecture that his whole reason for writing this Faith was that, affirming that there is one *hypostasis*, that is, one essence or substance, of the Trinity, he might defend himself against the calumnies of those who confessed three hypostases in the sense that had been approved by the Alexandrian Synod, and who, interpreting the force of this word according to their own opinion, accused of Sabellianism the others who interpreted it differently. Wherefore Faustinus presents his Faith to the Emperor in such a way that it agrees entirely with the Catholic doctrine of the Synod, but he wishes the words *hypostasis* and substance to be explained only by his own interpretation; which the very opening of the Formula indicates: "We set our seal to the confession of the first faith against Sabellius, and against those who, under the name of the Catholic Faith, defend impious words, saying that there are three substances."

And this is enough about Faustinus' Formula; whether its contents suit Lucifer anyone can easily recognise, simply by looking at the very words of the Faith and at the purpose for which it was published. But someone might say that a Faith actually written by Lucifer was taken over by Faustinus into his own Formula, with an opening and a close added, so that it might win more approval from its author himself. Yet Faustinus would not have kept silent about the name of Lucifer, whom in the petition (*Libellus precum*) he adorns with so much praise again and again. And finally, from what has been said so far, it can rightly be established that the Formula of Faith which we present here from the Ambrosian Codex is not to be attributed to Lucifer, who followed the Nicene Formula of Faith alone, who never wrote anything ambiguous or obscure about the Trinity, who confirmed the decrees of the Alexandrian Synod with his assent, who openly cursed the errors of Sabellius in the book *On Not Associating with Heretics*, and who was never brought under suspicion of any heretical error. That Formula of Faith, I say, is not to be attributed to him; rather, it was drawn from the Formula of Faustinus either by some ignorant man or by the Luciferian sect, corrupted with the ambiguous words we have noted, and either ignorantly or fraudulently ascribed to Lucifer, and about the fifth century it was afterwards inserted into the Ambrosian Codex with his name prefixed. I should like to add the following from the Preface to the first volume of Sirmond's Works, Venice edition, no. 2: "Some think that, together with that petition of Marcellinus and Faustinus, there was handed to the Emperors the Confession of Faith which, in the Code of Canons and Constitutions of the Roman Church, published twenty years ago in the Appendix to the Works of St Leo, edition of 1675, p. 138, is entitled 'The Faith of Faustinus the Presbyter sent to the Emperor Theodosius.' But since in the Preface of that same petition, which is the work of a schismatic, the Emperors are named as Valentinian, Theodosius and Arcadius, the petition must be put back to the year 383, in which Arcadius was proclaimed Augustus, and cannot be placed later than the year 392, in which Valentinian died; and this cannot agree with the year in which the Faith was published. Others judge the petition to be some years later than the Confession of Faith, which seems more likely." Let us now set out here a copy of each Faith side by side.
From the parchment manuscript codex of the Ambrosian Library marked I, 101, in the upper part.

HERE BEGINS THE FAITH OF ST LUCIFER THE BISHOP.

We believe in the Father, who is not the Son, but has the Son from himself without beginning, not made towards himself. And we believe in the Son, who is not the Father, but has the Father, from whom he is begotten, not made. And we believe in the Holy Spirit, who is truly the spirit of God. Hence we confess one substance of the Divine Trinity, because such as the Father is according to substance, such a Son he begot. And the Holy Spirit, not being a creature but the spirit of God, is not foreign to the substance of the Father and the Son, but is himself of the same substance with the Father and the Son, just as [he is] of the same Godhead. Here it ends.
THE FAITH OF FAUSTINUS THE PRESBYTER Sent to the Emperor Theodosius.

The faith written against the Arian heresy was sufficient. But because certain people, with a perverse mind, under the confession of that faith exchange [it for] impious words, stirring up odium against us as though we were defending the heresy of Sabellius, we set our seal in a few words to the confession of the first faith, both against Sabellius and against those who, under the name of the Catholic faith, defend impious words, saying that there are three substances; whereas the Catholic faith has always confessed one substance of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.

We believe in the Father, who is not the Son, but has the Son from himself, begotten without beginning, not made; and we believe in the Son, who is not the Father, but has the Father, from whom he is begotten, not made; and we believe in the Holy Spirit, who is truly the Spirit of God. Hence we also confess one substance of the Divine Trinity, because such as the Father is according to substance, such a Son too he begot; and the Holy Spirit, not being a creature but the Spirit of God, is not foreign to the substance of the Father and the Son, but is himself also of the same substance with the Father and the Son, just as [he is] of the same Godhead.

For let those who think we are Apollinarists know that we curse the heresy of Apollinaris no less than the Arian. And we are amazed that those can be approved as Catholics who confess three substances of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Even if they say that they do not believe the Son of God or the Holy Spirit to be a creature, yet they hold views contrary to the [true] faith, impiously, when they say that there are three substances; for it follows that those who confess three substances confess three Gods. This expression Catholics have always cursed.
